You know who has a very funny job right now? Joon Kim, the Wachtell Lipton partner and former federal prosecutor who was hired by Nvidia Corp. two weeks ago “to conduct a thorough and independent investigation” “ in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” When Kim got the job on Nov. 10, nothing was decided. In theory, Kim’s thorough and independent investigation could find that Huang did nothing at all wrong and should keep his job at Nvidia, or that he had, like, 37 affairs with spies and had to go. Nvidia’s board of directors would receive Kim’s report and use it to decide Huang’s fate. But then, two days later, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned, which presumably colored what the board expected from Kim’s report. A report concluding that Huang did nothing especially wrong would make the directors look bad: They had forced out a visionary founder, and erased $1.2 trillion of shareholder value, for no good reason. Can’t have that. After Nov. 12, Kim’s implicit job was to find as many affairs as possible. Not anymore, though! One assumes that he’s going through the draft today hastily deleting affairs. One is that you make a list of the stocks you want to buy, and you buy them. If you have a good reason to buy a stock, you buy it; if not, not. The default is not. If you have no opinions about a stock, you don’t buy it. The other is that you make a list of the stocks in the world, and for each stock on the list, you ask yourself: “Do I have a reason to overweight or underweight this stock?” The default is owning the market portfolio: If you have no opinions about a stock, or ambivalent or confused opinions, you tend to just own the average amount of the stock, its market capitalization weighting in the market portfolio. If you have reason to think that the stock is better than the market thinks it is, buy more of it. If you have reason to think that it’s worse than the market thinks it is, buy less of it, or zero, or go short. But you start from the premise that the market has a pretty good idea of what stocks to own, and that if you have no special information, then you should just do what the market tells you. I think it is fair to say that the second approach — defaulting to the market weight and overweighting or underweighting when you have reason to — was virtually unheard-of 100 years ago and is quite standard now. Many, many investors mostly buy index funds: They assume that the market knows better than they do, so they buy the stocks that the market likes. But many active investors use the same intellectual framework: They run large diversified portfolios and pick stocks to overweight and underweight against the background assumption that the default is the market weight. A company says it wants to raise $1 billion by selling 100 million shares at $10 each. Its bankers go out to investors, who put in orders for the shares. The bankers collect orders for, say, 700 million shares. “The IPO is seven times oversubscribed,” they say. [1] The IPO prices, and the bankers and company get together to “allocate” the IPO: There are orders for 700 million shares, but the company is selling only 100 million shares (actually 115 million with the greenshoe ), so most of the orders won’t get filled. The banks and company will favor some investors (long-term investors who understand the company’s story, the banks’ favorite clients, retail, whatever) and zero others (fast-money hedge funds that will flip the shares, etc.), but even the favored investors will probably get cut back. If you put in an order for 10 million shares, and the book is seven times covered, you’re not realistically going to get more than 5 million, and 2 million is more likely. But you know that, of course. If you have a sense that it will be a hot IPO — for instance because your salesperson at the bank says “this is a hot IPO and we’re getting a lot of demand” — you can scale up your order to try to get more shares. If you want 5 million shares, put in an order for 20 million. That way you’ll probably get cut back to 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 million. Sometimes you’ll mis-calibrate and end up with 1 million, or 10 million, either of which would be bad. (If you get 1 million, you’ll have to buy more when the stock starts trading, and if you got cut back to 1 million that probably means it will trade up. If you get 10 million, the reverse: You’ll have to sell when the stock starts trading, and if you got allocated so many shares, that’s a bad sign for demand.) But in a hot IPO, many investors are putting in orders for more shares than they want. [2] Or that is the stereotype. I have sometimes wondered if it applies to the new wave of mega-IPOs. I don’t know. But the flowchart is something like this: Anthropic’s board of directors would meet and decide what to do with him, weighing what various stakeholders — employees, suppliers, customers, governments, shareholders, etc. — want and their own sense of what would be best for the company and for the safe development of advanced artificial intelligence. Anthropic’s board has seven members, two of whom are Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, so that might be awkward. The board ultimately answers to a higher authority . Actually two higher authorities, or two and a half. Three of the seven board members are appointed by a “long-term benefit trust” made up of disinterested trustees whose job is to make sure that Anthropic builds AI safely for the benefit of humanity. Three are appointed by Anthropic’s seven co-founders. If you are an environmental investor, sometimes you put environmental concerns above shareholder returns. If you are a social investor, sometimes you put social concerns above shareholder returns. Governance is different: Governance means making sure that the managers of a company put shareholder returns above their own interests. If environmental, social and governance investing has good performance — if ESG stocks go up — it stands to reason that a lot of that performance would come from the governance. I don’t really want to argue for this analysis, which is debatable in various ways, [1] but there is something to it. “Governance” is, traditionally, about shareholder value, about how the profits of a company are split between its managers and its owners. Finance and legal academics noticed that, if a company makes a lot of money, the bandits in charge of the company could keep all the money for themselves and not give any of it to shareholders. “The premise behind modern corporate finance in general,” writes Jean Tirole on the first page of Chapter 1 of his corporate finance textbook , “is that corporate insiders need not act in the best interests of the providers of the funds.” Governance is about keeping an eye on the managers, so they do not become bandits, so the shareholders can get some of the money. This works very well in textbooks, but in the real world you have to take account of the particular skills and characteristics of particular bandits. Every so often, Elon Musk will go to the board of directors of Tesla Inc. and hint “hey, nice company you have here, it would be a shame if I were to go build robots elsewhere and break some stuff on my way out,” and the board will give him an extra trillion dollars. Banditry! But the shareholders do not complain, much, because Musk’s idiosyncratic personal involvement really is crucial to Tesla being worth a trillion dollars in the first place.
